lesson.title: Rise: The Vertical Half of Slope
lesson.summary: Rise is the vertical change between two points on a line, calculated by subtracting their y-coordinates, and it forms the numerator of the slope ratio.
lesson.body:
Slope compares vertical change to horizontal change, and rise is the name given specifically to that vertical change. Between any two points on a line, (x1, y1) and (x2, y2), the rise is calculated as y2 - y1, the difference between their y-coordinates. This is exactly the numerator of the slope formula covered in the previous chapter, isolated on its own so it can be discussed and measured independently of the horizontal change before the two are combined back together. Thinking of rise on its own, separate from run, mirrors how the y-coordinate was studied on its own before being paired with the x-coordinate to form a single complete ordered pair.

The sign of the rise carries directional meaning, the same way the sign of a y-coordinate does. A positive rise means the line moves upward between the two points, and a negative rise means it moves downward. A rise of zero means there is no vertical change at all between the two points, which happens along a perfectly horizontal line, one whose y-coordinate never changes no matter how far you travel along it in either direction.

Here is a worked example using two new points on the familiar line y = 3x - 2. Check that both points actually satisfy the equation first. At x = -1: y = 3(-1) - 2 = -3 - 2 = -5, giving the point (-1, -5). At x = 3: y = 3(3) - 2 = 9 - 2 = 7, giving the point (3, 7). Both points check out algebraically, so they are safe to use for this calculation. Now calculate the rise between them, going from the first point to the second: rise = y2 - y1 = 7 - (-5) = 7 + 5 = 12. So moving from (-1, -5) to (3, 7), the line climbs 12 units vertically, a fairly large jump.

Rise by itself, however, does not describe steepness completely. A vertical climb of 12 units could belong to a very steep line or a fairly gentle one, depending entirely on how much horizontal distance it took to achieve that climb. Twelve units of rise packed into a single unit of horizontal movement would be an extremely steep line, while the same 12 units of rise spread across 100 units of horizontal movement would be nearly flat. This is exactly why rise cannot stand alone as a measure of steepness and needs its horizontal partner to give it context. Two lines can even share the exact same rise between chosen points and still look completely different on a graph, simply because their runs differ.

That horizontal partner is called the run, covered in the next chapter, and it measures exactly how much horizontal distance separates the same two points used to calculate the rise. Once both rise and run are known for the same pair of points, they combine back into the slope ratio, rise divided by run, exactly as introduced in the slope chapter, closing the loop between vertical change, horizontal change, and overall steepness.
